narrative:
The 2026 Miami Marlins have been a team of dramatic swings and hard-fought moments, never quite settling into a comfortable identity but refusing to be counted out. They burst out of the gate in March with a 4-1 mark, Owen Caissie announcing himself with a walk-off blast on Opening Weekend that set a hopeful tone. April brought the first signs of inconsistency — an 11-15 month that featured both sparkling individual moments and devastating late-inning collapses, with reliever Pete Fairbanks becoming a recurring character in the wrong kind of stories.

May continued the struggles at 11-18, the team's lowest point of the year, but everything changed in June. The Marlins erupted for a remarkable 20-6 month — one of the best in recent franchise history — built on clutch hitting, timely defense, and a lineup that suddenly looked dangerous from top to bottom. Javier Sanoja emerged as the heartbeat of the offense, Jakob Marsee was seemingly on base every other inning, and the club strung together wins with a conviction that had been absent all spring.

July and August brought the team back to earth, hovering near .500 as the bullpen continued to betray them in high-leverage spots. Fairbanks and others surrendered leads that should have been closed, and a brutal three-game stretch against Milwaukee in mid-July and a Jarren Duran grand slam in late August were emblematic of a team that could not stop bleeding late. Yet the Marlins kept scratching — Xavier Edwards' clutch single in late July, Heriberto Hernández's go-ahead hit in August, and Joe Mack's sacrifice fly showed a lineup unwilling to fold.

September has been a tense, back-and-forth affair. At 80-82, the Marlins sit on the edge of relevance with games still to play. Javier Sanoja's thirtieth double in mid-September was a reminder of how far he has come as a player, and Esteury Ruiz's sharp extra-base hit the following day kept the offense humming. The road ahead is narrow, but in a season defined by improbable June and scattered heroics throughout, nothing about these Marlins suggests they are done making noise.

chapters.title: April Turbulence
chapters.description: The Marlins go 11-15 in April as promising offensive moments are repeatedly undercut by brutal late-inning pitching breakdowns.

chapters.title: The June Surge
chapters.description: Miami catches fire with a stunning 20-6 June, turning their season around with clutch hits and a suddenly locked-in lineup.

chapters.title: Treading Water
chapters.description: July and early August see the Marlins hovering near .500, trading clutch offensive moments for costly bullpen collapses.

chapters.title: Scratching and Clawing
chapters.description: Late August produces both gut-punch losses and gritty rallies as Miami fights to stay relevant heading into the final month.

chapters.title: September on the Brink
chapters.description: With their season on the line, the Marlins battle through September, led by Javier Sanoja's thirtieth double and Esteury Ruiz's timely hitting.
